I have encountered similar issues with LightmapGI and am happy to provide a sample scene if it will be of assistance.

I can reproduce this! I don't seem to be able to work around it by wrapping the scene in an opaque box which suggests it's not necessarily the rays slipping through cracks or something. Looking at the lightmap, it looks like the padding is bright white for some reason: I'm using my own UV2 unwrapper for most of the geometry in my level so I've been able to fix this by cranking the padding.
As far as I can tell it is not a padding issue as it appears here even with very wide padding: EXR:

Ok, I have a new theory about what is causing this. I'm currently experimenting with mesh generation and I've found this only happens along concave edges with split normals. I suspect what we're seeing here is the rays passing "around" the corner (pictured):
Here's a **better** comparison of split normals (bicubic filter is off this time): Smooth normals: Now the smooth normals are kinda smudging it a bit but the haloing is completely gone.

I tested the scene with two new meshes, each totally smooth-shaded and reproducing different scenarios that might be encountered in production. The first uses support loops to push the shading to the edges for a cheap beveled effect, and the second is simply subdivided so the shading follows the forms more accurately than large flat smoothed quads. In both cases the leaks persisted. Here's the updated project file: [LightmapSeamsBug.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30172575/LightmapSeamsBug.zip)
Can confirm with version 4.6.2. Is this a regression?

> Can confirm with version 4.6.2

It's also reproducible in 4.7.1

I had trouble importing the MRP to much older versions, and I noticed it had quite a few settings that were not the default on the light, environment and lightbake nodes, so I made a basic scene with these adjustments: - Node3D * WorldEnvironment (default settings) * DirectionalLight3D (shadows on, bias set to 0) * LightMapGI (default settings) * Imported 'ExposureOcclusionMetalMesh.glb' (shadows set to double sided) I tested with Godot 3.6.2, Godot 4.0 and Godot 4.6.2. These are the results: Godot 3.6.2: Godot 4.0: Godot 4.6.2: You can see in godot 3, there are issues present (peter panning effect despite bias set to 0), though I don't think I recognise the issue presented by the original poster. Godot 4.0 introduces the issue, and it persists up until 4.6.2, probably beyond it. I could be wrong though, and maybe what I'm seeing is unrelated to this issue.

@ibe-denaux Some settings were changed slightly from default to show the leaking better.
Namely the Directional Light is set to Static since shadowmaps (and issues inherent to them) are irrelevant. A blue sky was used to show that the leak isn't unique to direct light sources.
Godot 3 uses a CPU lightmapper that was mostly or completely rewritten to utilize the GPU in Godot 4, so it will perform differently. Good to know this leak might be a regression though.

> In 4.6 , you can still see there's light leaks in 4.6.2 , though they are minor, did you set a higher texel desity or lightmap quality, or is it the default?

All lightmapping settings are set to default and are the same across the tests.

This seems to be related to texture filtering/padding (tested in Godot 4.8): Nearest filtering: Bicubic filtering: Nearest but with supersamping (2x) enabled. Also shows a similar issues likely from the supersampling process (which presumably also uses some form of texture filtering in the downscaling process). All tests are done with denoising enabled and quality set to high. Linear filtering has the same issue as bicubic filtering has. Note that in the images in the opening post the bias is set too high (0.05 instead of the default of 0.0005) causing even larger light leaks that are also present when using nearest filtering. These are the results when correcting this setting: Nearest: Bicubic: (note the light leak in the back on the right).

Did some more testing and came across another interesting flaw in the lightmapper that might be related to this issue. When you remove the dilating step from the code you get a 1 texel wide black line along some of the seams: The grid here lines up with the texels. See https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/110700 These show up on texels that partially "go outside" their UV island but it only happens on one of two opposing sides of the quads. To visualize what seems to be happening when UVs don't allign with the texels grid: The grey grid are the texels, Red represents the final UVs in the lightmap, white represents the baked lightmap: What I would expect to happen would be that all texels the UVs touch would be filled like this: This on its own isn't a huge issue as the dilating step fills in these missing texels but when dilating from nearby UV islands can you end up with this: Faded colors represent dilated pixels. And because texture filtering will blend each pixels with the neighboring ones will this create what looks like light leaking from nearby islands even if there is a barely sufficient enough gap of two texels between the two island. And this is more common than you might think as Godot generates very tightly packed UV2's that mostly only have a 2-3 texel gap between each island if you bake at the default texel scale (which is already quite dense). Well within the danger zone.

One thing to note is that the leak occurs regardless of texel density or island spacing. Here's a test with a custom lightmap UV with far too much spacing and a Texel Scale of 24, resulting in a nearly-filled 2k lightmap. Although they may contribute I suspect the culprit is more than dilation or texture filtering bleed across islands.
Could you share that exact project? Would like to have a look at it to see if I could find the cause.
Nevermind, managed to recreate this on my own (still had some half-assed lightmap fixes in my code that did hide this issue somewhat).
@Skywolf285 would you mind to share those fixes? :)

It was this commit: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/437a9f10a14157126f28dfc62766fe81a2e43fe7 Want to stress this doesn't actually fix anything as removing the wire drawing step merely makes it less likely for the problem to occur. The only thing I kept is removing the 0.5 texel offset as that was a seemingly haphazardly merged PR that doesn't really do anything either other than, again, slightly mask the actual issue while also shifting the entire lightmap half a pixel making it slightly misaligned. With this, I also want to correct my previous post about the missing texel that gets filled in by the dilating step. That was caused by the removal of the wire drawing step. ### So what is the actual issue then? Whenever the center of a texel either lines up exactly at or slight past an edge, cast rays fall outside the geometry. It doesn't matter if the angle is greater, lower of exactly 90 degrees. It also doesn't matter if edge in question is the edge of an UV island or somewhere in the middle (although due to how the wire drawing step works is the former more likely to produce the issue). Light leaking happening at all edges, even shallow angled ones: The green glow is from an mesh emitting light below the surface. Showing it does cast rays outside the geometry and not missing rays all together (which then would be traced against the environment texture). In this case it seems to hit the bottom of the mesh (lightmapper doesn't care if a mesh if backface culled) which then reflects the light source below. **What I excluded so far:** The position map is correct. As in, the positions of the texels get properly aligned to the edges of the geometry. Whether that is desirable I'm not sure. Position output interpreted inside Blender (using geometry node). The dots are the position map, the geometry the mesh exported into Godot. Have spend dozens of hours by now trying to understand the lightmapper (am slowly getting there) and in `lm_compute.glsl` I though maybe this was causing issues. Idea being that a texel at an edge is smaller than this calculation would give: ``` vec3 position = texelFetch(sampler2DArray(source_position, linear_sampler), ivec3(atlas_pos, params.atlas_slice), 0).xyz; vec4 neighbor_position = texelFetch(sampler2DArray(source_position, linear_sampler), ivec3(atlas_pos + ivec2(1, 0), params.atlas_slice), 0).xyzw; if (neighbor_position.w < 0.001) { // Empty texel, try again. neighbor_position.xyz = texelFetch(sampler2DArray(source_position, linear_sampler), ivec3(atlas_pos + ivec2(-1, 0), params.atlas_slice), 0).xyz; } float texel_size_world_space = distance(position, neighbor_position.xyz) * bake_params.supersampling_factor; ``` But setting `texel_size_world_space` to a low number or 0 doesn't change anything. Which makes sense as I'm pretty sure this is only used for soft shadows against non-emissive light sources (point lights .etc) while my tests so far only test against emissive surfaces and the environment. Edit: Things I tried but forgot to mention: - Checked the normals debug texture outputted by `lightmapper_rd.cpp` - looked correct. - Force nearest filtering on the sampler used in `lm_compute.glsl` - made no difference. - Force a bias of 0 - Broke the lightmaps in other ways but didn't fix the leaking. Any suggestions (or solutions) on where to look would be appreciated!

Not sure if it is helpful, but some people reported on reddit that issues with light leaking[ disappeared on Windows if you switch from dx12 to Vulkan](https://www.reddit.com/r/godot/comments/1te2yr2/help_fixing_light_leaks_with_lightmap_gi/)
Leaking persisted with negligible change when baking in Vulkan for this scene.

Hey guys, I put together an AI assisted solution here: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/123341 

It was only possible because of your hard work here, and I hope it can be of use even if I can only take partial credit for it.

New discovery: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/110700 actually somewhat fixes light leaks: Current Godot behavior: With https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/110700 applied: The reason for this is that `lightmap_size_hint` either isn't set or isn't set correctly when a mesh doesn't have its UV2 generated during import (still looking into this). This PR estimates them which makes the lightmaps render at a more appropriate resolution (and because UV islands don't have their margin adjusted for the lightmap resolution do they leak into neighboring ones, creating these light leaks). To make it more confusing: if you enable generating UV2s during import, reimport and then disable it again and reimport again, will the "correct" `lightmap_size_hint` remain until you restart Godot. Meaning that your lightmaps might render perfectly fine until you return the next day to add more stuff to your level and things suddenly break on the next lightmap bake.
BTW I'm closing that PR because its Superseded by https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/123078. https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/110700 adds to much complexity
